evade.e: From Middle French évader, from Latin ēvādō (“to pass or go over; flee”), from ē (“out of, from”) + vādō (“to go; walk”).
evade.g: To get away from by cunning; to avoid by using dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to cleverly escape from.

evaluate.g: To draw conclusions from examining; to assess; to appraise.

evangelist.e: From Old French evangeliste, equivalent to evangel + -ist, from ecclesiastical Latin evangelista, from ecclesiastical Ancient Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistḗs, “bringer of good news”), from εὐαγγελίζεσθαι (euangelízesthai, “to evangelize”), from εὐάγγελος (euángelos, “bringing good news”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + ἀγγέλλειν (angéllein, “to announce”).
evangelist.g: An itinerant or special preacher, especially a revivalist, who conducts services in different cities or locations, now often televised.

evaporate.e: Participial usage up until Early Modern English.
evaporate.g: To transition from a liquid state into a gaseous state.

evening.e: From Middle English evenynge, evenyng, from Old English ǣfnung, from ǣfnian (“to become evening”), from ǣfen (“eve”) (from Proto-West Germanic *ābanþ, from Proto-Germanic *ēbanþs), corresponding to even + -ing.
evening.g: The time of day between afternoon and night.

evenings.g: In the evening, during the evening.

evenly.e: From Middle English evenly, evenliche, from Old English efenlīċe (“evenly, alike, equally”), equivalent to even + -ly.
evenly.g: So as to form a flat surface.

event.e: From Middle French event, from Latin ēventus (“an event, occurrence”), from ēveniō (“to happen, to fall out, to come out”), from ē (“out of, from”), short form of ex + veniō (“come”); related to venture, advent, convent, invent, convene, evene, etc.

eventide.e: From Middle English eventide, from Old English ǣfentīd, from ǣfen (“evening”) + tīd (“time”). By surface analysis, even + -tide.

ever.e: From Middle English ever, from Old English ǣfre, originally a phrase whose first element undoubtedly consists of Old English ā (“ever, always”) + in (“in”) + an element possibly from feorh (“life, existence”) (dative fēore).

everlasting.e: From Middle English ever-lasting (“(adjective) eternal, perpetual; constant; (adverb) eternally; (noun) eternity”), from ever (“at all times, always, constantly; eternally, perpetually; regularly; etc.”) + lasting (“continuing, lasting; eternal; etc.”). Ever is derived from Old English ǣfre (“ever”), possibly from ā (“always, ever”) + in fēore (“in life”).
everlasting.g: Lasting or enduring forever; endless, eternal.

evermore.e: From Middle English evermore (written as two words before 14th century), equivalent to ever + -more.

every.e: From Middle English every, everich, everych, from Old English ǣfre ǣlċ, ǣfre ǣġhwelċ. By surface analysis, ever + each or ever + which.
every.g: All of a countable group (considered individually), without exception.

everyday.e: From Middle English everidayes, every daies, every dayes (“everyday, daily, continual, constant”, adjective, literally “every day's”), equivalent to every + day.
everyday.g: Appropriate for ordinary use, rather than for special occasions.

everyone.e: An alteration of earlier everychone after every, from Middle English everichon. By surface analysis, every + one.
everyone.g: Every individual in a set; every person.

everything.e: From Middle English every thing; univerbation of every + thing.

everywhere.e: From Middle English eauerihwer, from Old English æfre + gehwær. By surface analysis, every + where.
everywhere.g: In or to all locations under discussion.

evict.e: From Middle English evicten, evycten, borrowed from Latin ēvictus, past participle of ēvincō (“to vanquish completely”).
evict.g: To expel (one or more people) from their property; to force (one or more people) to move out.

evidence.e: From Middle English evidence, from Old French, from Latin evidentia (“clearness, in Late Latin a proof”), from evidens (“clear, evident”); see evident.
evidence.g: Facts or observations presented in support of an assertion.

evident.e: From Middle English evident, from Old French evident, from Latin ēvidēns (“visible, apparent, clear, plain”) (compare Late Latin ēvideor (“to appear plainly”)), from ē (“out”) + videō (“see”), present participle vidēns, deponent videor (“to appear, seem”).

evidently.e: From Middle English evidently, evydently; equivalent to evident + -ly.
evidently.g: In a manner which makes the fact or conclusion evident; obviously; as may be clearly inferred.

evil.e: From Middle English yvel, evel, ivel, uvel, from Old English yfel, from Proto-West Germanic *ubil, from Proto-Germanic *ubilaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂up(h₁)élos, a deverbal derivative of *h₂wep(h₁)-, *h₂wop(h₁)- (“treat badly”). Alternatively from *upélos (“evil”, literally “going over or beyond (acceptable limits)”).

From Middle English yvele, yvel, ivel, from Old English yfele (“badly, evilly”), a derivative of the adjective yfel (“bad, evil”). Often reinterpreted as the noun in the later language (as in "to speak evil").

evildoer.e: From Middle English yvel doer; equivalent to evil + doer.
evildoer.g: A person who performs evil acts.
